sections.overview: The common nightingale is a small, ground-foraging Old World flycatcher whose celebrated song carries through European scrub in spring. It breeds across Europe and parts of western and central Asia, then crosses the Sahara to winter in sub-Saharan Africa.
sections.identification: Adults are about 15–16.5 cm long, and the sexes look alike in plumage. Brown upperparts, a reddish tail, pale unspotted underparts, a fine bill and relatively long legs give this secretive bird a plain, upright appearance; juveniles are spotted. British ringing samples put adult mass around 18–24 g.
sections.habitat: Breeding birds favour dense scrub and young woodland with low, leafy cover and patches of bare soil beneath. They place their nest on or close to the ground, concealed among leaves and stems; this structure provides cover and nearby foraging ground.
sections.diet: It takes insects and other small invertebrates, especially beetles and ants, searching through leaf litter and low vegetation with short hops and pauses. In late summer and autumn, berries and other fruits supplement this animal prey.
sections.behavior: Males produce loud, varied whistles, trills and bubbling phrases to attract females and advertise or defend a breeding territory. Night song is especially associated with unpaired males seeking mates; after pairing, males usually stop singing regularly at night, so not every individual sings nocturnally all season.
sections.reproduction: The female builds a low cup of dead leaves and grasses, lined with finer plant material, feathers or hair, and usually lays four or five eggs. She incubates them for about 14 days; downy, helpless chicks are fed in the nest and normally fledge at 11–13 days. Leaving the nest is not independence: young remain near cover while learning to forage and continue to rely on adults afterward.
sections.ecology: Ground-foraging nightingales take invertebrates, while raptors and mammals prey on them; low dense scrub gives cover to nests and newly fledged young.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment published in 2017, based on a 2016 assessment, classified the species as Least Concern. In Britain, BTO describes the localized breeding population as declining; deer browsing and scrub loss or maturation reduce suitable low cover, and winter-ground changes may also affect returning birds.
